newsitem.title: USA: Perot warns of "Watergate II" in last-minute blitz.
newsitem.headline: Perot warns of "Watergate II" in last-minute blitz.

text.p: Reform Party candidate Ross Perot ended his presidential campaign on Monday with a bombardment of television infomercials and warned of a Watergate-like constitutional crisis if President Bill Clinton is re-elected.

Perot, the billionaire candidate for the party he built with his own money, accused both major parties of selling themselves and American jobs to shadowy foreign interests and blasted away at Clinton's personal integrity.
He said another four-year term for Clinton would see criminal charges brought against the president and plunge the country into crisis.

"You must cast an informed vote tomorrow because we are on the verge of a Watergate II and a constitutional crisis," Perot said in election-eve infomercials which aired on ABC, CBS and NBC at a cost of $2 million.

"Would you hire a person facing criminal charges to babysit your children? Of course not. To paint the interior of your house? No, they might steal something," Perot said. "How could you ever consider voting for a person with pending criminal charges to be president of the United States?"
Reform Party aides described the television blitz as "two hours of saturation bombing" before Americans go to the polls.

Perot was way behind in the presidential race with most polls showing him stuck in single figures, but he was energized in recent days by indications of public concern over foreign campaign contributions and focused his attacks on Clinton.
Returning on Monday to his favorite campaign tool of television infomercials, Perot drove his point home for the final time.
"Why would you even think about voting for a president who violates the law, doesn't tell the truth and doesn't keep his promises?" he said.

But the feisty Texas businessman, who has so far this year failed to repeat the magic which won him 19 percent of the popular vote in 1992, did not specify what charges he expects to be brought against Clinton.

Several of Clinton's former associates were convicted in the so-called Whitewater investigation, which arose from questions about the failed Whitewater real estate venture in which the president and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton were investors.

The saga has dogged Clinton throughout his first White House term but neither he nor his wife have yet been indicted by special prosecutor Kenneth Starr, who has led the Whitewater investigation for the last two years.
Perot suggested that Clinton might pardon his jailed former business partners and associates.

The president also came under fire for allowing allegedly improper fundraising by the Democratic Party from Asian business interests. Clinton said there was no wrongdoing but called for campaign finance reform that included a ban on political contributions from foreign interests.
Perot said the Republican and Democratic parties are incapable of giving up the "corrupt" money that comes from special interest groups.
Campaigning in San Antonio earlier in the day he pushed his familiar themes of huge government debt and impending financial disaster if spending deficits are not trimmed.
He said Clinton's claims to have led an economic revival were misleading, and accused both major parties of exporting millions of good manufacturing jobs with bad trade agreements.
Perot spent about $70 million of his own money in his 1992 White House bid but this year opted to accept $29.2 million of federal funds.
